vignette: Layla was twelve when the wooden rod first met her shoulders in the narrow hallway. It was never preceded by warnings; her mother would simply lunge without explanation, pinning her against the wall until the strikes subsided. Layla stopped trying to describe the violence to relatives, finding that the terror remained trapped in her nervous system, impossible to translate into coherent language. When the memories of those evenings finally surfaced, her body automatically assumed the exact hunched posture of her childhood, shoulders rolled forward and spine rigid against an invisible pressure. Because the abuse was sudden, physical, and delivered from close quarters, she learned to brace her posture before a blow even landed, storing the event as a visceral blueprint rather than a narrative. Years later, working as a social ministry coordinator, those stored sensations resurfaced with relentless precision. During a staff meeting at the community center, a colleague’s coat brushing against the doorframe triggered an immediate defensive crouch. Layla reacted as if she were in danger again, her pulse spiking and her breath catching even though nothing was actually wrong. She began frequently looking behind her to check if someone was following, her eyes constantly scanning the ministry’s corridors for a looming figure. When a volunteer’s heavy footsteps echoed too closely, her irritability flared, resulting in a sharp, uncharacteristic outburst that left the room quiet and her face burning with shame. Whenever the bodily reenactment surged, bringing the unspoken physical memory of that hallway to the forefront, the threat response would ignite, flooding her with false alarms that danger was imminent. The raw intensity of those sensations drove her to alter her daily routine; she started avoiding work responsibilities that required sitting still, pacing the office instead. She made sure to stay near the exit of every meeting room, her attention fixed on the door handle as new faces entered, and she insisted never to be alone with another person, propping doors open during administrative tasks. The protective measures she adopted only fed the system forward. The false alarms and irritability, in turn, dictated her next retreats; the moment her nervous system spiked, she would flee to the perimeter of the room, cementing the avoidance that guaranteed the traumatic memories would never be safely processed. The more she avoided work or studied her caseload from a distance, the more unprocessed the memories lingered, waiting to surface as unbidden bodily reenactments during quiet moments. Her constant checking behind her only trained her brain to expect pursuit, making every shadow a potential attacker and fueling fresh waves of rage when recalled fragments finally broke through her defenses. This threat-driven hyperarousal kept the memory network primed, ensuring that each new false alarm would trigger another wave of physiological recall. Her colleagues noticed how she would abruptly end conversations, muttering that she needed to leave before someone crossed her line, and her relationships frayed as she pushed away the stability she had once built. Now, at fifty-one, Layla sits in a therapist’s office, her hands gripping the arms of the chair. She has come to believe that the world is still that narrow hallway, that she must anticipate the strike to survive it. What frightens her most is that her own anger might finally tip over into violence, that the rage she has swallowed for decades will escape and confirm her deepest fear: that she is fundamentally dangerous, just like her mother. She hopes, quietly, that she might learn to trust the present moment enough to stop bracing for a blow that never comes.
